comments.body:
Hi @willmcgugan, looked into this and can confirm it's still reproducible on current `main` (v15.0.0), not just the reporter's 12.6.0 from 2022.

**Root cause**: `BlockQuote.__rich_console__` renders its child elements via a single `console.render_lines(self.elements, ...)` call, which just concatenates their lines with no separator. `Markdown.__rich_console__` (the top-level document loop) explicitly inserts a blank line between block-level elements based on each element's `new_line` flag. That's why sibling paragraphs outside a block quote get a blank line between them, but paragraphs rendered inside one via `BlockQuote` never do.

**Fix**: render each child of the block quote separately and apply the same `new_line`-based spacing rule the top-level loop uses, so the blank line is prefixed with `▌` (matching how a blank blockquote-continuation line is actually written in source markdown).

I have a small diff ready: the core fix, a regression test, and updates to two existing snapshot tests that were asserting the old (buggy) spacing. Full test suite passes clean against it.

Per `AI_POLICY.md`: this fix was developed with AI assistance (Claude, via Claude Code). I reviewed and verified the diff myself, including reproducing the bug and confirming the fix before writing this. Happy to open a PR if this approach looks right to you.

issues.title: [BUG] rich.progress.Progress transient option not working when exception is thrown within context
issues.body:
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

**Describe the bug**

When an exception is thrown from within the Progress context, the progress bar fails to exit correctly and leaves a blank line even when transient=True.

To be fair, my use case is pretty niche.

```python
class DownloadContext:
    """Context for Downloader."""

    def __init__(self, progress: Progress):
        """Context for Downloader."""
        self.progress = progress

    def foobar(path):
        # if file exists then skip download
        if path.is_file():
            raise SkipDownloadException

        # do download

class Downloader:
    """Download files or webpages with rich progressbar."""

    @contextmanager
    def begin(self):
       
        status: DownloaderExitStatus

        with Progress(transient=True) as prog:
            try:
                yield DownloadContext(prog)
            except SkipDownloadException:
                status=DownloaderExitStatus.SUCCESS_SKIPPED
            else:
                status=DownloaderExitStatus.SUCCESS_DOWNLOAD
    
       # print appropriate message based on status

downloader = Downloader() 
with downloader.begin() as context:
    context.foobar()
```

When ``foobar()`` runs without throwing an exception python exits my ``with Downloader.begin() as context`` block, evaluates the  ``else`` part of my try/except/else block and the progress bars disappear like they're supposed to but when ``SkipDownloadException`` is thrown in ``foobar()`` it goes to the ``except SkipDownloadException`` statement like expected and prints my messages, but the progress bars leave behind a blank line. I think this might just be a unique edge case, but maybe a more seasoned python programmer can tell me if I'm misunderstanding the ``with`` statement, generators, or exceptions or something.

comments.body:
Hi, I've reproduced this and traced it to the `decode()` method in `rich/ansi.py`.

The split regex `(?<=\n)` keeps `\n` at end of each chunk, which `decode_line` strips with `rstrip("\n")`. But on CRLF input (`\r\n`), the `\r` remains — and then `line.rsplit("\r", 1)[-1]` takes only what's **after** the last `\r`, which is empty, producing blank lines.

The fix is a one-liner in `decode()`: strip `\r` from each line before passing to `decode_line`:

```python
# current
for line in re.split(r"(?<=\n)", terminal_text):
    yield self.decode_line(line.rstrip("\n"))

# fixed
for line in re.split(r"(?<=\n)", terminal_text):
    yield self.decode_line(line.rstrip("\r\n"))
```

This preserves the existing `rsplit("\r", 1)` carriage-return handling in `decode_line` while not leaving a stray `\r` that wipes the line content. Happy to submit a PR if this approach looks good.

I've fixed this issue by modifying `rich._log_render.LogRender.__call__`.

https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/46cebbb032f920eb096efbaf23cdc6fe9dd541f7/rich/_log_render.py#L32-L70

The changes I made were two:
1. replace both `file://`s with `file:///` in style f-strings.
2. add `link_path = link_path.replace('\\', '/')` at the beginning of the function definition.

Why this works:

1. According to the URI specification (RFC 8089 I believe) , the file URI scheme has the format:

`file://<host>/<path>`

`<host>` represents the machine where the file resides.

For local files on the same machine, the `<host>` must be empty (or localhost).

When the host is empty, the URI becomes `file:///` (three slashes), followed by the absolute path.

Most Windows applications (including VS Code, File Explorer, and Windows Terminal) follow the RFC and require the triple-slash format for local file links. The double-slash format is either rejected or interpreted incorrectly (e.g., trying to open a network share named C:).

2. The URI standard requires that path separators be forward slashes (/), even on Windows. Backslashes are not allowed in URIs because they have special meaning as escape characters.


So the log links generated by the following sample will work as expected:
```python
import logging

from rich._log_render import LogRender
from rich.logging import RichHandler

# Store original method
_original_log_render_call = LogRender.__call__


def _patched_log_render_call(
    self,
    console,
    renderables,
    log_time=None,
    time_format=None,
    level='',
    path=None,
    line_no=None,
    link_path=None,
):
    """Patched version that fixes Windows file links."""

    # Fix Windows paths for the link
    if link_path:
        # Convert backslashes to forward slashes
        link_path = link_path.replace('\\', '/')
        # Add the third slash (will be used in the f-string below)
        # The original code does: f"link file://{link_path}"
        # We need: f"link file:///{link_path}"
        # So we prepend a slash to link_path
        link_path = '/' + link_path

    # Call original with modified link_path
    return _original_log_render_call(
        self,
        console,
        renderables,
        log_time,
        time_format,
        level,
        path,
        line_no,
        link_path,
    )


# Apply the patch BEFORE creating handlers
LogRender.__call__ = _patched_log_render_call

# Now configure logging normally
logging.basicConfig(
    level='NOTSET',
    format='%(message)s',
    datefmt='[%X]',
    handlers=[
        RichHandler(
            show_path=True,
            enable_link_path=True,
            rich_tracebacks=True,
        )
    ],
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.info('Test message with clickable link')

```

### Alter the `Confirm.validate_error_message` attribute

```python
Confirm.validate_error_message = "[prompt.invalid]Per favore digita S o N"

Confirm.ask("Confermare?", choices=["s", "n"])
```

**Pro**:
- Since this is a quick and dirty hotfix, it's less verbose than the preceding workaround

**Cons**:
- Changes all subsequent calls to the `Confirm` class

Add a `validation_error_msg` parameter (or something like that) to the `Confirm.ask` method which overrides the `Confirm.validate_error_message` each time, so that the following works as expected:

>>> from rich.prompt import Confirm

Confermare? [s/n]:
Please enter Y or N
Confermare? [s/n]:

Confermare? [s/n]:

Confermare? [s/n]:

issues.title: [BUG] Text.from_ansi: NUL byte between ESC and "[" bypasses re_ansi and reaches the terminal as a live escape sequence
issues.body:
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

**Platform**
Tested against rich v15.0.0 with kali's default terminal, qterminal.

**Describe the bug**
`Text.from_ansi` uses re_ansi to tokenize ANSI escape sequences. The regex expects ESC (0x1B) to be immediately followed by a recognized byte, so a NUL (0x00) inserted between ESC and "[" prevents a match. `_ansi_tokenize` then yields the whole sequence as a literal plain-text token.

`Text.append()` passes it through `strip_control_codes()`, but that only strips codes 7, 8, 11, 12 and 13, not NUL (0) or ESC (27). The raw ESC NUL [2J bytes therefore survive in the Text and are printed. Many terminal emulators ignore NUL bytes, so they reconstruct and execute the sequence.

**PoC**
(Note: This will erase the entire terminal. Ensure your terminal has text on the screen to observe the clear-screen command)
```
from rich.text import Text
msg = "\x1b\x00[2J"
text = Text.from_ansi(msg)
print(text)
```

**Impact**
Tools that pass untrusted data (e.g. file contents from a network share) through from_ansi can emit unintended control sequences: screen clearing, cursor movement, and output spoofing.

**Suggested fix**
The regex could account for NUL after ESC, and `strip_control_codes` could be extended to also strip NUL bytes that survive outside of a successfully matched sequence, as defense in depth.

issues.title: [BUG] Traceback.extract loops forever when __cause__ and __context__ form a cycle
issues.body:
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

**Describe the bug**

`Traceback.extract` loops forever when an exception chain forms a cycle through `__cause__` and `__context__`.

`Traceback.extract` follows `__cause__`, then `__context__`, until neither is set. It guards only against an exception that is its own cause (the fix for #3708) and against repeated exception-group members. So when two or more exceptions form a cycle, for example A's `__context__` is B and B's `__cause__` is A, the loop never ends. `stacks` grows by one entry per pass and memory grows without bound. `Console.print_exception()`, `Traceback.from_exception(...)` and `RichHandler(rich_tracebacks=True)` never return.

Ordinary code builds such a chain: re-raising an exception with `raise error` inside the handler of an exception that was raised `from` it. When Python sets `__context__`, it breaks cycles that run only through `__context__` links, but not cycles that pass through `__cause__`. The chain is legal, and the standard library prints it, because `traceback.TracebackException` keeps a `_seen` set and prints each exception once.

Minimal example (runs unmodified):

```python
import traceback

from rich.console import Console

error = ValueError("inner")
try:
    try:
        try:
            raise error
        except ValueError as exc:
            raise RuntimeError("outer") from exc
    except RuntimeError:
        raise error  # error.__context__ is the RuntimeError, whose __cause__ is error
except ValueError:
    traceback.print_exc()  # the standard library prints the chain and returns
    print("stdlib done", flush=True)
    Console().print_exception()  # rich never returns
    print("rich done", flush=True)
```

**Expected:** rich prints each exception in the chain once, as `traceback.print_exc()` does, and returns.

**Actual:** `stdlib done` prints, then `print_exception()` never returns and memory keeps growing (RSS about 186 MB at 3 s and about 339 MB at 6 s) until the process is killed. `rich done` never prints. Under `timeout 8` the script exits 124.

**Impact:** an application that logs errors through `RichHandler(rich_tracebacks=True)` blocks the logging thread permanently on such an exception. In an asyncio server, that thread is the event loop, so every request stalls. Several frameworks install that handler by default.

**Suggested fix:** in the chain walk at the end of `extract`, keep a set of the exceptions already visited (as `TracebackException` does with `_seen`), and stop following `__cause__`/`__context__` into one already in it. The existing `_visited_exceptions` set could carry it. That would also subsume the `cause is not exc_value` check.

**Platform**
<details>
<summary>Click to expand</summary>

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64), CPython 3.13.7 and 3.12.15, rich 15.0.0. The same walk is unchanged on `master` at 9d8f9a372c. This isn't terminal-specific: it reproduces with output redirected to a file, where `is_terminal` is `False`.

```
$ pip freeze | grep rich
rich==15.0.0
```

</details>

*This report was drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code). I ran the reproduction and checked the results by hand.*

Fix: track the exceptions already rendered and stop the walk when one repeats, same idea as the stdlib _seen set. Normal cause/context chains and ExceptionGroups are untouched.

Fix is on bunnysayzz/rich branch fix/traceback-exception-cycle-4238 (commit 63d939b3), with a regression test. The test hangs on the original code and passes with the fix; the full tests/test_traceback.py suite is green (23 passed, 1 skipped).

**Describe the bug**

Importing any Rich submodule fails before application startup when the current working directory exists but `os.getcwd()` raises `PermissionError`.

`rich/__init__.py` captures `_IMPORT_CWD` at import time and catches only `FileNotFoundError`. On macOS, `getcwd()` can raise `PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted` when the responsible application lacks access to the current directory. This is closely related to #2197 and its fix in #2212. That fix handles a deleted cwd, but not other `OSError` cases.

```python
import os
from unittest.mock import patch

with patch.object(
    os,
    "getcwd",
    side_effect=PermissionError(1, "Operation not permitted"),
):
    import rich
```

    _IMPORT_CWD = os.path.abspath(os.getcwd())
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^
PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted

**Describe the bug**

Indexing styled `Text` with a negative integer returns the correct character but loses its spans. Positive indexing and a negative slice preserve the style. Python's negative-index semantics suggest `text[-1]` should be equivalent to `text[len(text) - 1]`, including formatting.

```python
from rich.text import Text

text = Text.from_markup("[bold]hello[/bold]")
print(text[4].plain, text[4].spans)
print(text[-1].plain, text[-1].spans)
print(text[-3:].plain, text[-3:].spans)
```

Actual output:

```text
o [Span(0, 1, 'bold')]
o []
llo [Span(0, 3, 'bold')]
```

Expected: `text[-1]` returns a bold `o` like `text[4]`.

At `rich/text.py:198-209`, `__getitem__` uses the negative offset for Python string indexing (which succeeds), but compares that same negative offset with nonnegative span boundaries (which never match). Indexing once to keep Python's `IndexError` behavior and then normalizing the negative offset before checking spans appears to fix it. Could @willmcgugan confirm that preserving spans for negative integer indices is the intended behavior? I have not opened a PR pending the approval required by `AI_POLICY.md`.

**Platform**

Windows, CPython 3.10.1, Rich 15.0.0 installed editable from default-branch commit `9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f`. Pure API example; terminal rendering not required. Searched open and closed issues/PRs for negative Text indexes and lost styles without finding a matching report.

Negative integer indexing retrieves the correct character from self.plain, but span matching still uses the original negative offset. Since span boundaries are non-negative, the styles are lost.

In rich/text.py, inside Text.__getitem__(), I retrieve the character first, then normalize the negative offset before checking spans:

character = self.plain[offset]
if offset < 0:

**Describe the bug**

Rendering an `xml.etree.ElementTree.ParseError` whose message is an `ExpatError` raises a secondary `TypeError`, masking the original XML parse error. This occurs with the pure-Python ElementTree parser used by defusedxml (see tiran/defusedxml#105). The reproduction below needs only Rich and the standard library:

```python
import io
import sys
from xml.etree.ElementTree import ParseError
from xml.parsers.expat import ExpatError

from rich.console import Console
from rich.traceback import Traceback

try:
    raise ParseError(ExpatError("syntax error"))

```

TypeError: str or Text instance required, not ExpatError('syntax error')

`ParseError` subclasses `SyntaxError`. `Traceback.extract()` currently stores `exc_value.msg` directly in `_SyntaxError`, although it already has a `safe_str()` helper for the main exception value. Would normalizing this field with that helper, with tests for non-string messages and a failing `__str__`, be an acceptable fix?

macOS arm64, CPython 3.13.5, Rich 15.0.0. Also reproduced using the current `main` checkout. Output is directed to `StringIO`, so no terminal-specific rendering is involved. The original end-to-end example also fails with defusedxml 0.8.0rc2 and structlog 26.1.0. Explicitly selecting `structlog.dev.plain_traceback` is a verified workaround for that integration.

## Root cause

In `rich/traceback.py`, the `Traceback._render_stack()` handler builds a `_SyntaxError` from any `SyntaxError` subclass:

```python

    ...
    msg=exc_value.msg,

console = Console()
try:
    raise ParseError(ExpatError("syntax error"))
except ParseError:
    console.print_exception()  # TypeError
```

Coerce the message to `str` in `rich/traceback.py`:

+        msg=str(exc_value.msg),
```

issues.title: Console.print(text) silently drops Text's own justify unless justify= is also passed to print()
issues.body:
**AI disclosure (per AI_POLICY.md):** this was investigated and written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic). I independently reproduced it against a fresh clone of `main` myself before filing — repro below, runnable standalone, no dependencies beyond Rich itself.

## Summary

A `Text` object's own `.justify` attribute is silently dropped when the `Text` is passed directly as a top-level argument to `Console.print()`, unless `justify=` is *also* passed to `print()` itself — even though `Text.__rich_console__` documents/implements `self.justify` as taking priority over the console-level default.

## Reproduction

```python
from rich.console import Console
from rich.text import Text
import io

buf1 = io.StringIO()
Console(file=buf1, width=20).print(Text("hi", justify="center"))
print(repr(buf1.getvalue()))
# -> 'hi\n'                    <- not centered, despite Text's own justify="center"

buf2 = io.StringIO()
Console(file=buf2, width=20).print(Text("hi", justify="center"), justify="center")
print(repr(buf2.getvalue()))
# -> '         hi         \n'  <- only works if justify is ALSO passed to print()
```

## Root cause

`Console._collect_renderables()` (`rich/console.py:1550-1554`, inside `check_text()`) funnels every `Text` object through:
```python
sep_text = Text(sep, justify=justify, end=end)   # justify = print()'s own kwarg, default None
append(sep_text.join(text))
```
`Text.join()` (`rich/text.py:788`) builds the merged result via `self.blank_copy()`, where `self` is the *separator* `sep_text` — so the joined result inherits the **separator's** `justify`/`overflow`/`no_wrap`, silently clobbering whatever the joined-in `Text`'s own `.justify` was set to.

The same `Text` object centers correctly when wrapped in `Panel(...)` or `Group(...)`, because those containers call `console.render()` on the inner `Text` directly, bypassing this join path — so the bug is specific to passing a `Text` as a direct top-level argument to `Console.print()`.

## Checked

`gh search issues --repo Textualize/rich` for "justify" (30+ related hits reviewed) — found related-but-distinct issues (#460 `console.log` missing a `justify` kwarg entirely, fixed 2020; #3948/#4021 `Table` title justify with `soft_wrap`) but nothing matching this specific "`Text.justify` silently dropped by `print()`" defect. Appears unreported.

Happy to put together a PR (something like: preserve the joined item's own `justify`/`overflow`/`no_wrap` when it's a single `Text` and `print()`'s own `justify` wasn't explicitly passed) if this is confirmed as worth fixing.

issues.title: [BUG] Text.wrap(console, width=0) raises ValueError in chop_cells (range step 0)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

`Text.wrap(console, width=0)` raises `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero` for ordinary (single-cell) text. The same call with double-width text does not crash, so the behaviour is inconsistent.

The crash is in `rich/cells.py::chop_cells`, whose single-cell fast path builds `range(0, len(text), width)`:

```python
if _is_single_cell_widths(text):
    return [text[index : index + width] for index in range(0, len(text), width)]
```

With `width == 0` the step is `0`, which `range` rejects. The general (wide-character) path below it has no such step and returns without raising, so `chop_cells("hello", 0)` crashes while `chop_cells("你好", 0)` does not.

It reaches the public API through `Text.wrap` -> `_wrap.divide_line` -> `chop_cells` (the `word_length > width` fold branch, taken by any non-empty word when `width` is 0). Width 0 is reachable when text is rendered into a zero-interior region (a table column squeezed to zero, a nested panel with no room, a console sized to 0); Rich otherwise degrades gracefully at tiny widths, so a hard crash here stands out.

**Minimal repro** (runs as-is):

```python
import io
from rich.console import Console
from rich.text import Text

console = Console(file=io.StringIO())
Text("hello world").wrap(console, 0)   # ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero
```

Lower-level, showing the single-cell vs wide-char inconsistency:

```python
from rich._wrap import divide_line
divide_line("hello", 0)   # ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero
divide_line("你好", 0)     # returns normally
```

Traceback:

```
  File ".../rich/text.py", line 1239, in wrap
    offsets = divide_line(str(line), width, fold=wrap_overflow == "fold")
  File ".../rich/_wrap.py", line 59, in divide_line
    folded_word = chop_cells(word, width=width)
  File ".../rich/cells.py", line 338, in chop_cells
    return [text[index : index + width] for index in range(0, len(text), width)]
ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero
```

**Suggested fix**

Guard `chop_cells` against a non-positive width (return `[text]` when `width <= 0`, since text cannot be chopped into zero-width lines). comments.body:
Hi folks, I also just came across this with [rich-codex](https://github.com/ewels/rich-codex) and ended up digging into it a bit. I think @shiba2046's guess 3 years ago was right: `textLength` is too small.
Explanation The cause is in `Console.export_svg`. Three values are derived from the same segment, but one of them measures in characters where the other two measure in cells: Width calculation: https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/rich/console.py#L2512 Cells - correct: https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/rich/console.py#L2520 Characters - incorrect: https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/rich/console.py#L2534 `x` advances by cells and the background `rect` is sized in cells, but the `` element declares `textLength` from `len(text)`. If the cell width differs from its character count (CJK, emoji, combining marks etc.) then the value is wrong.
Reproduction ```python import io, re from rich.console import Console from rich.cells import cell_len CHAR_WIDTH = 20 * 0.61 # char_height * font_aspect_ratio, Rich's defaults def text_length(svg, needle): for m in re.finditer(r']*textLength="([\d.]+)"[^>]*>([^<]*)', svg): if needle in m.group(2): return float(m.group(1)) for text in ["a✨b", "a漢b", "aéb", "漢字漢字"]: console = Console(record=True, width=20, file=io.StringIO()) console.print(text, highlight=False, markup=False) got = text_length(console.export_svg(title=""), text[:1]) want = CHAR_WIDTH * cell_len(text) print(f"{text!r:12} chars={len(text)} cells={cell_len(text)} " f"textLength={got:6.2f} expected={want:6.2f}") ``` On 15.0.0: ``` 'a✨b' chars=3 cells=4 textLength= 36.60 expected= 48.80 'a漢b' chars=3 cells=4 textLength= 36.60 expected= 48.80 'aéb' chars=4 cells=3 textLength= 48.80 expected= 36.60 '漢字漢字' chars=4 cells=8 textLength= 48.80 expected= 97.60 ``` So the double-width characters come out too narrow, and a combining accent (`e` + U+0301, 2 characters but 1 cell) too wide. The last row is this issue — `漢字漢字` is declared at half the width it needs, so the glyphs overlap.
### Suggested fix ```diff - textLength=char_width * len(text), + textLength=char_width * text_length, ``` I'll put in a PR to fix this. Note that this only affects SVG export.

issues.body:

**Describe the bug**

Three tests in `tests/test_console.py` don't run, or don't assert anything. Two of them are hiding assertions that no longer match Rich's current behaviour, so this isn't only a tidy-up — restoring them surfaces two stale expectations.

Checked against `master` (`9d8f9a37`), Python 3.12, macOS.

---

**1. `test_soft_wrap` is defined twice (lines 48 and 604)**

The second definition wins and the first never runs. They are different tests:

```python
# line 48 -- never collected
def test_soft_wrap() -> None:
    console = Console(file=io.StringIO(), width=20, soft_wrap=True)
    console.print("foo " * 10)
    assert console.file.getvalue() == "foo " * 20

# line 604 -- this is the one that runs
def test_soft_wrap() -> None:
    console = Console(width=10, file=io.StringIO())
    console.print("foo bar baz egg", soft_wrap=True)
    assert console.file.getvalue() == "foo bar baz egg\n"
```

Renaming the first one to run it makes it **fail**: it expects `"foo " * 20` (the input duplicated) with no trailing newline, but Rich emits `"foo " * 10` plus `\n`. The expectation looks wrong rather than the code — the second test asserts the same "soft wrap doesn't wrap, and ends with a newline" behaviour and passes. So the shadowed copy appears to be an obsolete leftover.

**2. `test_force_color` is defined twice (lines 953 and 968) — this one loses parametrization**

```python
# line 953 -- never collected, and it's parametrized
@pytest.mark.parametrize("env_value", ["", "something", "0"])
def test_force_color(env_value) -> None:
    console = Console(file=io.StringIO(), _environ={"FORCE_COLOR": env_value})
    assert console.is_terminal

# line 968 -- this is the one that runs
def test_force_color() -> None:
    ...
    assert console.color_system in ("truecolor", "windows")
```

`pytest --collect-only` currently shows **one** `test_force_color`; it should be three parametrized cases plus the unparametrized one.

Restoring the parametrized version fails on `env_value=""`, and that one is legitimately obsolete: it dates from #2467 (2022), while `9175392a` ("New environment var", 2025-03-28) deliberately changed `is_terminal` to

```python
force_color = environ.get("FORCE_COLOR")
if force_color is not None:
    return force_color != ""
```

so an empty `FORCE_COLOR` is now explicitly *not* a terminal, per <https://force-color.org/>. The shadowing is why CI never flagged the contradiction. The `"something"` and `"0"` cases still pass and are worth keeping.

**3. `test_tty_interactive` builds a `Console` and never asserts on it (line 1063)**

```python
# Force tty compatible, force not interactive
console = Console(
    file=io.BytesIO(), _environ={"TTY_COMPATIBLE": "1", "TTY_INTERACTIVE": "0"}
)

# Bytes file, Unknown value of TTY_INTERACTIVE should still auto-detect
console = Console(file=io.BytesIO(), _environ={"TTY_INTERACTIVE": "foo"})
assert not console.is_interactive
```

The first `console` is overwritten before use, so the `TTY_COMPATIBLE=1` + `TTY_INTERACTIVE=0` case — the interesting one, where the two vars disagree — is never checked. The behaviour is correct today (`is_interactive` is `False`); the assertion is just missing.

**Proposed fix**

Happy to open a PR that:

1. deletes the obsolete shadowed `test_soft_wrap` (line 48);
2. restores the parametrized `test_force_color` under a distinct name, dropping the now-invalid `""` case and keeping `"something"`/`"0"`, and renames the other to reflect what it checks (`color_system`, not `is_terminal`);
3. adds the missing `assert not console.is_interactive` in `test_tty_interactive`.

Point 2 is the one worth a maintainer opinion before I write it: I've assumed the 2025 `FORCE_COLOR=""` change is intended and the old test is stale, but tell me if you'd rather keep the old assertion and treat it as a regression.

macOS, Python 3.12, `rich` at `9d8f9a37` (version 15.0.0).

issues.title: [BUG] Line breaking breaks at NBSP (U+00A0) — doesn't respect non-breaking space semantics
issues.body:
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

## Describe the bug

Rich wraps text by tokenizing it into "words" with `re_word = re.compile(r"\s*\S+\s*")`
(rich/_wrap.py). In Python's default (Unicode) regex mode, `\s` matches U+00A0
NO-BREAK SPACE, so Rich treats NBSP as a word boundary and a line-break opportunity.

This violates the Unicode line-breaking semantics of NBSP, which is explicitly a
**non-breaking** space: text must not break at an NBSP. Any content that uses NBSP
to keep a run together (e.g. a kaomoji like ``( ´・ω・` )``, or manually joined
tokens) gets split across lines anyway.

### Minimal example

```python
from rich.console import Console

# Kaomoji whose internal spaces are NBSP (U+00A0) so it should NOT be split.
kaomoji = "( ´・ω・` )".replace(" ", "\u00a0")
# A long passage that exceeds the console width and must wrap onto several lines,
# so we can observe where the line breaks happen.
long_text = "this is a long passage that exceeds the console width and must wrap"
console = Console(width=10)
console.print(kaomoji + "  " + long_text)
```
- **Expected**: the kaomoji stays intact on a single line as one unit; wrapping happens
  only at the regular spaces in the following long passage.
- **Actual**: Rich breaks *inside* the kaomoji at the NBSP positions, scattering the
  kaomoji across multiple lines (the long passage after it is irrelevant to the bug —
  it only forces wrapping so the break inside the kaomoji becomes visible).

### Root cause

`rich/_wrap.py`:

```python
re_word = re.compile(r"\s*\S+\s*")
```

`\s` (Unicode mode) includes U+00A0; `\S` excludes it. So a "word" is a run of `\S`,
which stops at NBSP — making NBSP a break point. A NBSP should be part of the
unbreakable word, not a separator.

### Expected behavior / minimal fix

Treat NBSP as a non-breaking space: include it in the word token, never a break
point.

```python
# separator = whitespace except NBSP; word = (non-ws or NBSP)+
# the two branches \S and \xa0 are mutually exclusive -> linear time, no backtracking
re_word = re.compile(r"[^\S\xa0]*(?:\S|\xa0)+[^\S\xa0]*")
```

issues.body:
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

**Describe the bug**

I have some code that I was debugging and was confused by the appearance of attributes called `awehoi234_wdfjwljet234_234wdfoijsdfmmnxpi492` and `_fields`. This was pretty hard to debug. It turned out that these are both added by `rich`.

* `awehoi234_wdfjwljet234_234wdfoijsdfmmnxpi492` is used to test objects for [auto-vivifying attributes](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/rich/pretty.py#L649). If the test succeeds (e.g., the [`Box`](https://github.com/cdgriffith/Box) class), the new attribute is left on the object.

* `_fields` is used to test if an object [appears to be a `namedtuple`](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/rich/pretty.py#L573). The comment asserts that “[i]t is possible to craft an object that passes this check and isn't a namedtuple, but there is only a minuscule chance of this happening unintentionally.” I don’t think that’s true; any object that auto-vivifies attributes will pass the check.

In my view, a library designed for debugging output (which `rich` is quite good at) should do its best to not modify the objects it is displaying, and if it does modify them, to be as obvious as practical about where the modifications came from.

I would suggest:

1. Because the sentinel `awehoi234_wdfjwljet234_234wdfoijsdfmmnxpi492` is controlled by `rich`, change it to something that makes its provenance clear, say `_rich_fake_attribute_test`.

2. Remove the sentinel attribute if it’s successfully created, e.g. with `delattr()`.

3. Test for the presence of `_fields` in a way that avoids false positives on auto-vivifying objects, e.g. with `__getattribute__()` instead of `getattr()`.

Thanks for `rich`, it’s been very helpful.

Hi! I investigated this issue and prepared a fix along with a regression test.

The issue occurs because Rich probes objects for auto-vivifying attributes using `hasattr()` with a temporary attribute name. For objects implementing `__getattr__`, this probe creates the temporary attribute and leaves it on the object after inspection.

My change removes the temporary probe attribute after the check, and I added a regression test to verify that `pretty_repr()` no longer leaves the probe attribute behind. I also verified that the existing `tests/test_pretty.py` test suite still passes.

Hi! I'd like to work on this. Per the AI policy I'm seeking maintainer approval for the approach before opening a PR (which would disclose AI assistance — Claude Code — with the work reviewed and owned by me).

I reproduced all three problems on current `master`:

1. `pretty_repr()` leaves `awehoi234_wdfjwljet234_234wdfoijsdfmmnxpi492` in the `__dict__` of auto-vivifying objects (e.g. `Box(default_box=True)`).
2. `_is_namedtuple()` similarly vivifies `_fields` onto such objects (the second junk attribute you found).
3. A `tuple` subclass with an auto-vivifying `__getattr__` returning a tuple false-positives as a namedtuple.

**Proposed fix** (minimal diff, verified locally — full `test_pretty.py` suite passes):

- In `traverse()`: after the `hasattr(obj, <probe>)` check succeeds, best-effort `delattr(obj, <probe>)` in a `try/except`, so the probe attribute is not left on objects that auto-vivify it. (Fixes 1.)
- In `_is_namedtuple()`: look up `_fields` on `type(obj)` instead of the instance. Real namedtuples define `_fields` on the class, so detection is unchanged, but instance-level `__getattr__` is never triggered — no mutation and no false positive. (Fixes 2 and 3.)

I'd keep the probe attribute name as-is to minimize the diff, but happy to also rename it to something provenance-clear (e.g. `_rich_fake_attribute_probe`) if preferred — with the `delattr` cleanup the name only matters in the rare case where cleanup fails.

Would this approach be acceptable?
